webTitle: ‘He should resign’: unease in Republican Max Miller’s Ohio district amid domestic abuse allegations

fields.headline: ‘He should resign’: unease in Republican Max Miller’s Ohio district amid domestic abuse allegations
fields.trailText: Voters in the red district are concerned with congressman’s alleged behavior and political future ahead of the midterms
fields.bodyText: David Griffith was a registered Republican for years. But on Sunday evening, he watched the Ohio congressman Max Miller stumble through an 18-minute statement in which the lawmaker attempted to defend himself against allegations of domestic abuse against his ex-wife and infant child. What Griffith saw and heard, he said, was a person that bore no resemblance to the Republican party he once supported. “What I saw was a person who needs help,” said Griffith, seated at a bench in a community park in Wooster, a quiet town of 26,000 people situated at the southern end of the beleaguered Miller’s congressional district. Though he has been critical of Donald Trump for years, last May Griffith ended his formal affiliation with the Republican party. “At this [midterm] election, I’m voting a straight Democratic ticket,” he said. “I’ve never done that before.” Across Miller’s largely red district, Republicans are deeply concerned with their representative’s alleged behavior and political future. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of the Republican Ohio senator Bernie Moreno, has accused Miller of pointing a gun at her head, pouring hot water on her and potentially breaking their two-year-old daughter’s collarbone. Emily Moreno has also alleged Miller physically attacked her attorney and another legal representative, and filed for a restraining order on her lawyer’s behalf. Emily Moreno and Miller are now locked in a bitter custody battle. On Sunday, Bernie Moreno called for Miller to resign in an X post after years of silence on the issue: “He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.” Miller, who faces an election this November, has denied any allegations of domestic abuse. In his statement on Sunday, he blamed the so-called leftwing media and his former wife for initiating a campaign to sully his name. On Tuesday, he attempted to defend himself further on Jake Tapper’s evening show on CNN, likening his fight to that of Trump’s when the president also faced sexual assault allegations. “The police are not investigating it; ask yourself, why aren’t they investigating these things?” he said. Before specific details of the allegations against Miller were recently made public and before Senator Moreno’s calls, Miller was expected to easily retain his seat, with pollsters suggesting in June the district leans Republican by five points. Miller, 37, who had previously served as a presidential aide during Trump’s first administration, was endorsed by Trump in 2021 during his first campaign. But this week, reports emerged that the president’s support for Miller may be waning. The final day the Ohio Republican party could replace Miller with another candidate, if it decides to do so, is 12 August. Bill Heck, vice-chair of the Republican party of Medina county, which lies inside Miller’s district, wouldn’t say if he thinks the congressman should resign. “There is so much stuff flying around that we have not been able to decipher what’s real and what’s not. What we’re trying to determine right now is how much of this is credible and how much he can refute and recover from,” he said. But he did concede that Republican voters in Miller’s district are worried. “I think a lot of our members and our steadfast Republicans are concerned,” he said. “I’m sure the president does not want to lose that seat. With 92 days left [to the election] it’s going to be really difficult for anybody to come in and take over the position – if appointed.” A host of other Republican party county organizations and groups across Miller’s district, including the women’s branch of the Republican party of Cuyahoga county, asking if they thought the congressman should resign, did not respond to requests for comment on the situation. While Miller as the incumbent won his 2024 congressional election by a 15% margin, a Democrat and an independent candidate split the vote between them. In November, Miller faces Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker from Brook Park, a Cleveland suburb. “The district leans Republican, but it is not so overwhelmingly Republican that a Democrat could never win,” says Justin Buchler, an associate professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. “If you combine a midterm election moving everything nationwide towards the Democrats with a weak Republican candidate, that could be enough for the seventh district to flip. Miller is weakened at the moment, so if he tries to stay in the race, that helps Poindexter, and if Miller withdraws, then without a strong replacement, that still helps Poindexter.” ‘He hasn’t engaged with our community’ A former Marine Corps reserve, Miller, who is seeking a third congressional term, has a long history of allegations of violence towards women, including from the former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, who accused him of pushing her against a wall and slapping her when the two were dating. (Miller has denied the allegation.) In north-eastern Ohio, the Miller family is known as one of the most powerful and respected in the region. Max’s grandfather, Sam, who died in 2019, was an esteemed Cleveland real estate mogul and philanthropist. Sixty miles south of Cleveland, Wooster, the county seat of largely rural Wayne county, was once a heartbeat of the industrial midwest. The collapse of the local jobs market in the early 2000s and accompanying economic decline that followed over the past two decades has fueled resentment locally that Trump has long since tapped into. In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won 70% of the vote in Wayne county. Wooster hasn’t elected a Democratic mayor for decades. “If the [Republican] party followed the standards we did, then I’d say he should resign,” says Bill Bailey, a former judge and the chair of the Wayne county Democratic party. “In my view, the Republican party is more concerned about retaining votes than they are about enforcing any kind of standards.” He says he doesn’t believe Miller’s claims of innocence, nor do many typically Republican voters. In Wayne county’s primary elections held last May, Bailey says about 1,600 registered Republican voters chose independent candidates and another 500 Republicans picked Democrats. “He hasn’t engaged with our community,” says Bailey of Miller. “I doubt that the average person would recognize him on the street.” For Griffith, who runs a local Facebook group called Defending Democracy and believes that the Republican party should support the US’s allies overseas, Miller represents everything that’s gone wrong with the party. “I have to believe that people get involved in public service because they want to do good, regardless of party,” he says. “Max Miller is not one of those people.”

webTitle: Democrats look forward after progressive El-Sayed victory in Michigan | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Democrats look forward after progressive El-Sayed victory in Michigan
fields.trailText: Abdul El-Sayed is latest leftwing candidate to capture nomination for November’s midterm elections. Plus: gender parity in Latin America’s city of cycling
fields.bodyText: Good morning. The progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed has won the Democratic primary for the US Senate in Michigan. Despite many backing his opponent, Haley Stevens, in the race, leading Democrats are now uniting behind the former public health official with the goal of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement. What does El-Sayed’s victory mean for the Democratic party? Though a contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits, his rise could serve as a revision to the political establishment’s prior playbook of requiring candidates to run from the center in swing-state politics. What do the Democrats need to retake the Senate? Republicans currently control the chamber with 53 lawmakers. The easiest path for Democrats to take back the Senate requires holding on to their seats in Michigan and Georgia while ousting Republicans from blue state Maine as well as three other red states. Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director In a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts, Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). As Donald Trump’s third pick to run the CDC, Schwartz will take the reins of the agency amid public concern over an outbreak of cyclosporiasis and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s hesitancy towards vaccines. What was the vote? Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination. Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups Investigations from Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Legal Agenda have determined that Israel deliberately and directly attacked the Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. Deliberate attacks on civilians is a war crime. Khalil, 42, was killed while Faraj, 21, was injured. What has Israel said about the attack? Israel said it “regrets any harm caused to journalists” and that the journalists were killed “as part of a series of events” during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed. How many journalists have been killed in this conflict? Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office. In other news … Senior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light to violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank with policies that began with Trump rescinding sanctions on his first day in office. Nato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday. Donald Trump’s legal team is pushing to block a court order that would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster. The Cambridge professor Jason Arday, accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career. Stat of the day: 90% of US adults listed groceries and food costs as their top cost-of-living concern A new survey found that a majority of Americans agree that the rising cost of living is a significant barrier to achieving a better life. According to a new survey of more than 30,000 adults from across the country spanning generations and economic classes, 60% of respondents said they wanted greater financial security but 40% described themselves as either “getting by but financially vulnerable” or “struggling to meet basic needs”. The Filter recommends: 32 things worth buying from Nordstrom’s anniversary sale Nordstrom’s annual sale, which runs until 9 August, includes more than 22,000 items across home, fashion, beauty, travel and more. The Filter crew has sifted through all of them to find the 32 deals they endorse, on top brands ranging from Le Creuset to Ray-Ban. Don’t miss this: Black college gymnasts in a divided South Gymnast Nyla Aquino is one of the University of Georgia’s brightest stars, leading her team to a resurgent sixth-place finish at the 2026 NCAA championships. But she and other Black athletes competing in the Southeastern Conference are striving to make their mark in a region of historical anti-Black prejudices, in a time when diversity, equity and inclusion programs and voting rights are under attack. “No matter how well I do, someone’s going to be racist,” she said. …or this: Achieving gender parity in Latin America’s city of cycling While Bogotá records nearly 900,000 bicycle trips each day – more than any other city in Latin America – less than a third of cycling journeys are taken by women. City officials are looking to change that. “Many older women come here because they were never allowed to ride a bicycle as girls,” said Sergio Prieto, who helps to oversee Bogotá’s Bike School. “They were told bikes were for men, that women shouldn’t be riding them. Here, those barriers and stereotypes are left behind.” Climate check: How the human-driven climate crisis fuels Canada’s deadly wildfires A new study conducted by World Weather Attribution found that the human-driven climate crisis amplified the conditions that led to fires blazing across Canada. Burning coal, oil and gas has overheated the planet and caused climate-influenced conditions to occur every two to six years in the Northwest Territories and every six to 15 years in Ontario. There are 700 fires burning in Canada at present. Last Thing: How well do you know the latest dating terms? Fresh dating trends seem to emerge every week in this age of app-based romance. Some terms such as “ghosting” or “catfishing” have become part of the modern parlance. But how familiar are you with other dating trends? Take this quiz and find out. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now. Get in touch If you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please email newsletters@theguardian.com

webTitle: Why making Anthony Fauci the enemy will harm US public health for years

fields.headline: Why making Anthony Fauci the enemy will harm US public health for years
fields.trailText: Republicans are trying to scapegoat the infectious disease expert, even as they have gutted healthcare amid outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis and Ebola
fields.bodyText: Katie Miller, an erstwhile Trump administration official and wife of Stephen Miller, once relied on Dr Anthony Fauci to get through Covid. Now, she’s calling for his imprisonment – a reversal that illuminates the politicization of Fauci and of public health writ large, a trend that could have major repercussions for America’s preparedness for future crises. A US Senate committee will vote on Thursday morning over whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after the physician and former public health official invoked his fifth amendment rights during a Senate hearing last week focused on Fauci’s actions during the Covid pandemic. The invocation of the worst days of the Covid pandemic comes as midterms loom and the administration struggles to address several infectious outbreaks, including cyclosporiasis and Ebola. Rand Paul, a senator, released contemporaneous notes that Fauci took during his time in public office, which Paul called Fauci’s diary, that reveal the confusion and fear of the time and illuminate the private episodes of a man who became known as America’s doctor. “By focusing entirely on one human being and by calling him all sorts of names, including ‘evil’, and by calling for him to be jailed, it abdicates Republicans’ own responsibility in the US response to the pandemic, which was under President Trump,” said Gavin Yamey, director of the Center for Policy Impact in Global Health at Duke University. “I think that this is all aimed at riling up the base ahead of the midterms and at washing their hands of any culpability themselves in the mass death event of Covid.” And it comes after substantial cuts to the public health infrastructure; misinformation has spread at the highest levels of the government, and growing outbreaks of measles, whooping cough, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and more. “This is an extraordinarily good way to distract people from the very deliberate destruction of the US public health system,” Yamey said. Like most Americans, Miller turned to Fauci for advice during the pandemic. As communications director for then-vice president Mike Pence, she was involved in the White House Covid-19 response. Fauci, who served as the director of the National Institute for Allergies and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), was also the chief medical adviser to seven presidents over three decades. Fauci described Miller warmly, writing that she was “great (tough, smart, but great)” on 25 March 2020, and that they “laugh at each other” in the Situation Room on 6 May 2020. When Miller tested positive for Covid, Fauci called to check on her several times a day. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote on 9 May 2020. Later, Fauci wrote that he had directly contacted Miller’s pediatricians to discuss the baby’s care. It is perhaps not surprising that Miller would turn to Fauci, as many others in the country also relied on his advice and insight during a deeply uncertain and terrifying time. But her actions contrast with the intensity and speed at which Covid was politicized – and the extent to which Fauci would draw conservatives’ ire, even years later. In February and March 2020, Miller was reassessing communications from the Covid taskforce, and Fauci was told to stand down on media appearances until he received clearance again. “That’s the episode that got tagged ‘muzzling Fauci’,” said Céline Gounder, editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News and a member of the Covid transition team under Biden. Soon after “deciding how much of Dr Fauci the public gets”, Miller was getting regular check-ins from Fauci on her own health, Gounder pointed out. “The same expertise: she’s rationing public access, but it’s available to her in private.” By April 2020, the pandemic was already being heavily politicized. The administration released plans for states to reopen, and President Trump posted a series of tweets encouraging supporters to “LIBERATE” blue states such as Minnesota, Michigan and Virginia. In late April, nearly half of Republicans (47%) surveyed by Pew Research Center said the pandemic was “made a bigger deal than it really is”. By June, that figure was 63%, and it rose to 66% in September. Republican attention to pandemic coverage went from 48% in March to 43% in late April to 35% by early June, while Democrats did not see any such changes. Spring 2020 looked similar across America; schools, for instance, were closed at about the same rate in red and blue states. But that changed by the fall, when “local partisanship predicted which districts would remain remote better than local Covid incidence did”, Gounder said. Those decisions were made not by Fauci, as he has been accused, but by about 13,349 public school districts, she pointed out in her newsletter, Underlying Conditions. “The more interesting story to me is who had private access to federal scientific expertise, what that access was worth in 2020, and what those same people have said about that expertise since,” Gounder said. She also pointed to early access to experimental treatments for Covid for Trump and his inner circle, nearly two months before they were available to the public. “A president publicly minimized a virus he was privately treated for with a drug the public couldn’t get,” Gounder said. Even after conservatives began publicly opposing his recommendations, the Millers still turned to Fauci for support. Fauci recounted speaking with Miller multiple times in October 2020, after her husband tested positive for Covid and she was traveling. “Spoke to her at Houston airport and after she landed,” he wrote on 6 October 2020. “Am on phone frequently with Katie and Stephen,” Fauci wrote on 31 December 2020. Katie Miller has since come out forcefully against Fauci. On the Covid taskforce, “Fauci cared more about virtue signaling than science,” Miller wrote in September 2025 in an apparent reference to wearing a face mask. In June, she said “he should be in jail”. After Fauci’s notes were made public, Miller claimed Fauci used the pandemic to “maximize his popularity”, and she endorsed calls to prosecute him. She told Notus she kept Fauci close so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”, though she didn’t specify what Fauci might leak. “Dr. Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponized my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandize himself,” Miller posted on Thursday, adding that “this man should be in prison”. Fauci has led the US through epidemics and pandemics over the decades: anthrax attacks in 2001, HIV, Sars, Ebola, Covid-19 and more, and he co-authored one of the most esteemed internal medicine textbooks. “We lose a lot when we see Republicans vilify Tony Fauci,” Yamey said. The US wasn’t unsafe because of Fauci’s leadership, Gounder said. “It wasn’t safe to leave home because a novel airborne virus was circulating in a population with no immunity, no vaccine, and no treatment.” And the Trump administration’s politicization and mismanagement “raised the toll”, she added. The trials facing Fauci make it less likely that others will step forward to guide public health, now or during a crisis. There were 1,499 harassment events across 583 local health departments between March 2020 and January 2021, and 222 officials left the field because of the targeting, Gounder pointed out. About 71% of the public health workforce reported at least one symptom of burnout and 20% reported near-constant symptoms in a 2024 survey. Three senior CDC leaders resigned last August over politicization of the agency, and one was fired for refusing to “rubber-stamp” Robert F Kennedy Jr’s anti-vaccine policies. The same month, a man fired more than 180 rounds into the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) campus because of misinformation about the Covid vaccine. He killed a police officer, David Rose. “If you’re 40 and choosing between US government service and industry, that’s now part of the math, not just the vast differences in compensation,” Gounder said. Yamey said he worried “that’s going to put future public health leaders off”. And there is an overwhelming amount of work to be done in addressing current public health crises and decades of repair to come. “But we will get there,” Yamey said. “We will all roll up our sleeves and build back, and hopefully build back better.”

webTitle: Thursday briefing: ​Is this the final whistle for Gianni Infantino at Fifa?

fields.headline: Thursday briefing: ​Is this the final whistle for Gianni Infantino at Fifa?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: Global football’s governance crisis is exposing ​a​ long history structural flaws, ​and as federations revolt and officials resign the sport faces a reckoning at the highest level
fields.bodyText: Good morning. In every pub where I watched this summer’s World Cup unfold, two motifs were shared by supporters. Yes, football was coming home, and also the (frankly more firmly held belief) that Gianni Infantino was a wrong’un. As in matchday stadiums, boos would routinely erupt when cameras cut to the Fifa boss; a proper panto villain. Regardless, he looked poised to cruise to victory in next year’s vote for Fifa president, despite this competition’s controversies – Fifa’s jaw-dropping, unprecedented overturning of US striker Folarin Balogun’s red card after Donald Trump’s lobbying chief among them. Undeterred, more than 200 of Fifa’s 211 member associations still backed his fourth term. Then last week, his Fifa Forward Enterprise plans were revealed: Infantino’s scheme to flog a stake in Fifa competitions to profit-seeking investors. World football has reacted with revolt, resignations and strongly worded statements. A growing chorus wants Infantino out. Yesterday, he gathered Fifa bigwigs for crisis management. But how did the gatekeeper of the beautiful game make things so ugly? That’s the topic for today’s First Edition, answered with the help of Guardian reporter Paul MacInnes, who has closely followed Infantino’s tenure. First, this morning’s headlines: Five big stories UK news | A woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden, central London, police said. Education | Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career. Ukraine | Nato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday. Middle East crisis | Iran and Oman have reached an understanding on ⁠the geographic coordinates for a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, and ⁠a joint announcement ⁠is being finalised provided certain third parties do not interfere, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said. US news | Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan, becoming the latest leftwing candidate to capture the party’s nomination ahead of November’s midterm elections. In depth: ‘It’s hard to dispute that football’s legitimacy is being undermined’ Barely two days after details of Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) emerged, came Infantino’s first major blow. Last Thursday, European football’s governing body Uefa announced its members had unanimously voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until FFE was scrapped. Of the six regional federations, two others soon expressed disdain at the proposals. Carlos Cordeiro, a senior Infantino adviser, announced he was quitting. Fifa chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been “deceived”. Pressure mounted until the weekend, when Fifa relented and scrapped the proposal. This backtracking hasn’t dispelled dissent. Uefa says it’s lost confidence in Infantino. Legendary Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger – a key Infantino hire at Fifa – said abandoning FFE was “absolutely necessary and beyond question”. Meanwhile Fifa’s secretary general wrote of “a sad and reproachable series of events” and that individuals “come and go” in a leaked internal memo. Jordan’s football chief has accused Infantino’s administration of “blackmail”. Portugal icon Luís Figo didn’t hold back, labelling Infantino’s actions “the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed”. At least four countries have now withdrawn their support for his reelection, with England set to follow suit, and more expected. “Many would like him to resign on principle,” says Paul, “but that hasn’t happened.” Yesterday, after a meeting in Morocco, Fifa confirmed that Infantino will remain as president. In a statement, which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team. “Currently, it feels like the pressure has dropped slightly,” Paul tells me. “There’ll be discussions about how the ante is upped again. If he doesn’t fall quickly, nations might assume he won’t go, cut their losses and stick with him. Without a well-established rival and widespread withdrawal of support, he’ll likely win re-election.” Because, despite the sleaze, when it comes to cold hard cash, Infantino has proven effective. This year’s World Cup generated $15bn – a tripling under his leadership. “Infantino has proven himself an elite executive when it comes to his priority: generating more revenue,” says Paul. In his rhetoric, at least, Infantino talks of boosting funds to footballing nations. And for the lesser-resourced, non-European football associations, this extra cash is gamechanging, even if Infantino’s $40m offer to those who backed his plans looked remarkably bribe-like. *** The clean-up candidate It’s hard to believe that Infantino was elected as a clean-up candidate. In 2015, after the US Department of Justice indicted 14 Fifa figures for racketeering conspiracy and corruption, Fifa’s last president, Sepp Blatter, announced his resignation. Blatter had been caught up in a long-running corruption case, alongside Uefa boss Michel Platini. The pair were accused (then acquitted, twice) of misappropriating £1.7m of Fifa cash. All of this, and the highly controversial awarding of the 2018 and 2022 World Cups to Russia and Qatar respectively, made Blatter’s position untenable. There was a gap at the top of world football and with Platini out, no obvious European successor. (Of Fifa’s nine permanent presidents, eight have been European). Enter Infantino, then second-in-command at Uefa. Central to his pitch was World Cup expansion. He had a message to world football, Paul says. “It’s not our money, it’s yours. And Fifa will make more for you.” It marked a rhetorical shift, with “a sense post-Blatter that execs had been lining their own pockets.” Looking to Europe, he offered another promise. “We’re going to clean the stables,” Paul recalls, “introduce new governance structures.” Infantino was perceived as a strait-laced Swiss bureaucrat – an image he projected. On his victory in 2016, he spoke of change. “Fifa has gone through sad times, moments of crisis. But those times are over,” he said. “We enter now a new era. We’ll restore the image of Fifa and make sure everybody will be happy with what we do.” *** A quick backlash Scandal came thick and fast. His election campaign first: Infantino declared spending €500,000 of Uefa funds to drum up support, but sources suggested the figure was closer to €1m. Fifa’s ethics committee began to investigate; Infantino organised the removal of its chair and members. Weeks after taking office, he was named in the Panama Papers, pulled into his own corruption scandal. There was a criminal probe after “indications of criminal conduct” in Switzerland. Swiss prosecutors subsequently closed their investigations, satisfied that suspicions against Infantino had been “invalidated”. “These stories have been endless,” says Paul. Take the Qatar World Cup, which Infantino inherited. Infantino committed to protecting human rights and remedying failures. These were widely documented, but no compensation fund was created. Fifa refused to act on fan safety in Qatar, where same-sex sexual acts are criminalised. Meanwhile Infantino goaded critics with that monologue: “Today I feel Qatari, today I feel Arab, today I feel African, today I feel gay, today I feel disabled, today [like] a migrant worker.” “That’s where it properly kicked off,” says Paul. “He became a real antagonist in the eyes of football fans.” Infantino’s awarding of the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia was widely criticised. His 2022 proposal to make the World Cup biennial (which, he claimed, could stop migrants from finding “death in the sea”) was botched. He invented a Trump-placating peace prize. In fact, he’d even attempted an FFE style ploy before. His 2018 proposal to fatten up the Club World Cup with private investor cash was “sprung on people with no consultation and little notice,” says Paul, adding that it “saw huge backlash before Infantino backed down.” *** The future of Fifa What incentivised Infantino to try to push through FFE has caused speculation. His multimillion pound salary and ample perks, already come with status that offers him access to the world’s most powerful figures. There were reports that Infantino might have eventually headed up FFE at a basic salary of $30m but Fifa have denied discussions on this have taken place. But this mess isn’t exclusively of Infantino’s (or Blatter’s) making. Paul has been speaking to academics, lawyers and football officials. “There’s a shared view reform is needed.” Many point to the need to break Fifa up: “Organising the biggest football tournament, while also regulating it, is untenable,” says Paul. Others see this as a chance to address inequality and elitism in the game. And European figures are also manoeuvring to push for external Fifa regulation. When doping scandals threatened to delegitimize sport, national governments and governance bodies founded the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada). “It’s hard to dispute that football’s legitimacy is being undermined,” says Paul. “Wada proves sporting organisations needn’t mark their own homework.” There are suggestions that the EU, OECD or even the UN should play a role, to “create a body outside football to handle complaints when they arise. So many complaints against Infantino have just disappeared. Someone needs to be able to hold Fifa accountable.” What else we’ve been enjoying I thought Symeon Brown was excellent in yesterday’s Long Wave newsletter, on Britain’s booming Black bourgeois class and why Brits just can’t seem to acknowledge it. Poppy Five US states held midterm primaries this week, with significant successes for progressive candidates. This explainer from Chris Stein on the Guardian’s US politics team helped me get a grip on the results. Michael I enjoyed Arwa Mahdawi’s take on the Trump officials who won’t just … focus on their actual jobs. Poppy My boyfriend is a real anchovy-head, and cans of surplus fishy oil often float in our fridge for days before eventual binning. No longer, with this salsa verde recipe from Tom Hunt I’m making as I type. Michael I was also thoroughly ruffled by our profile on the Phillipines’ so-called “Cockroach Lord”. Poppy Sport Cycling | Race favourite Demi Vollering won a three-way sprint to claim stage five at the Tour de France Femmes. Football | Eva Olid has described being appointed as the Manchester United Women head coach as a dream come true, after signing a two-year contract until 2028 with the option of a further year. Boxing | The former heavyweight world champion Joseph Parker ⁠said on Wednesday tnat he had been cleared to fight ⁠again after failing ⁠a dope test last October. The front pages “Academic resigns amid plagiarism accusations”, is the Guardian’s front page today, the Telegraph writes “Cambridge professor quits after false claims”, the Times has “Plagiarism row professor resigns from Cambridge”, and the Mail’s headline is “‘Plagiarism professor’ resigns as Cambridge investigate”. The Express writes “Early release is a ‘betrayal’ of hero police officer”, and on a similar topic, Metro has “My lad’s still serving time after phone theft in 2005”. Elsewhere, The FT leads with “China begins global tax hunt reaching back decades as fiscal pressure grows”, the Sun has “West End stab rampage”, and the Mirror, on new mental health centres, writes “Help is on the way”. The Latest Is Ukraine facing a major anti-missile shortage? At least 17 people were killed and more than 40 injured in another round of deadly Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has pleaded for more air defence weapons, saying ballistic missile interceptors ‘could have saved the lives of those killed today’. For months, Ukraine has been warning about shortages after Donald Trump backtracked on his promise to let Ukraine manufacture missiles locally. In response to the attack, the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen said ‘Russia must pay’ – but will it? Lucy Hough talks to the Guardian’s Russia affairs correspondent, Pjotr Sauer. Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Olaoluwa Olowu photographed amateur boxer Elizabeth Boakye in Accra after noticing that the city’s visual culture of boxing overwhelmingly celebrated men. Wanting to place a woman within that public archive, she returned with Elizabeth and positioned her beneath a mural of a male fighter. The portrait reflects both the visibility of male boxers and the absence of women, while acknowledging Elizabeth’s work with the national team, the Black Hitters. The image forms part of Women Who Fight, Olowu’s project documenting Ghana’s women boxers and ensuring they enter the sport’s visual record. Olowu says: “Elizabeth’s presence speaks to the women who are also part of the sport but are rarely represented in the same way.” This piece is part of our Women behind the lens series. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. webTitle: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan primary victory is the latest win for progressives challenging establishment-backed Democrats – as it happened

fields.headline: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan primary victory is the latest win for progressives challenging establishment-backed Democrats – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public-health official, won the Democratic nomination for the US Senate seat in Michigan, narrowly defeating Haley Stevens. He will now face Republican Mike Rogers in a must-win race for Democrats. Donald Trump launched a racist tirade against El-Sayed, mocking his Arabic name and claiming that his criticism of Israel’s killing and mistreatment of Palestinians could only be motivated by antisemitism. “He doesn’t love Israel. He doesn’t love Jewish people. He hates them. He hates them with a passion that burns in his heart and is not a fricking thing he can do about it,” Trump said. At a rally in Nevada, Trump praised Jim Marchant, an election conspiracy theorist who is running to oversee Nevada’s elections as its secretary of state. Faced with a malfunctioning teleprompter, Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, joked at Trump’s expense: “Unlike a certain world leader, I do not view this as a conspiracy.” Robert F Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services has provided a copy of Dr Anthony Fauci’s phone to a Republican-led Senate panel investigating the doctor’s role as a senior advisor on the response to the Covid-19 pandemic to presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden, the Wall Street Journal reports. Kennedy, wrote a conspiratorial book attacking Fauci in 2021 that sold more than a million copies – thanks in part to blurbs from fellow non-scientists Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan, Alan Dershowitz and Tony Robbins. Bernie Sanders, the socialist Vermont senator who has backed a number of left-wing candidates in Democratic primaries this year, said on Wednesday that he is unlikely to endorse Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist who has led in recent opinion polls of the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor. Bernie Sanders, the socialist Vermont senator who has backed a number of left-wing candidates in Democratic primaries this year, said on Wednesday that he is unlikely to endorse Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist who has led in recent opinion polls of the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor. In an interview with Pod Save America, Sanders was asked about the Wisconsin primary by Jon Favreau. “I noticed you haven’t yet endorsed in the Wisconsin governor’s race. What’s your thinking there, and might you endorse?” Favreau asked. “I don’t think so,” Sanders replied. “I met a Francesca a couple of years ago, I was in Wisconsin, and she seems very, very nice. But again, this is a race I’m just not that familiar with.” “We have not gotten involved in many governor’s races,” he added. “I think we did one in Maine, with Troy Jackson. You know, obviously, my major concern right now is seeing that we have a Senate and a House that is going to stand up to Trump.” “So, as of now, we have not been involved in that race,” Sanders went on, referring to his political movement which is pushing the Democratic party he caucuses with but never joined, to the left. Ahead of next week’s primary election, Hong, a Wisconsin state lawmaker who is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, has been pressed to explain social media posts in 2020 in which she supported defunding and abolishing the police. In the wake of the police shooting of Jacob Blake in August of 2020, Hong wrote on Twitter: “I support defunding the police as a first step towards abolishing the police.” Two months later, after federal prosecutors said there was not enough evidence to charge the officers who shot Blake with excessive force, Hong posted: “How is 7 bullets in the back not excessive force. Police exist to uphold white supremacy. Defund then abolish. Reform can’t be an option. My heart breaks for the trauma the Blake family and their community continues to endure. #BlackLivesMatter” During an interview with Pod Save America earlier this week, Favreau, a former speechwriter for Barack Obama, told Hong that “since Republicans will spend an ungodly amount of money um to defeat you, if you’re the nominee, to try to defeat you, I just want to make sure you have the best possible answers to what’s coming.” He then asked her to explain how her views on policing “had evolved since 2020”. “My views have only become stronger in that I’m serious about public safety, and I will not abolish the police,” Hong replied. “My views are that people are struggling right now and need basic eeds met and I want to focus on stopping violent crime and giving law enforcement the resources and the training that they need, but ensure that we are also holding accountable law enforcement that does not follow the law.” “Do you still believe that police exist to uphold white supremacy?” Favreau asked. “No,” Hong replied. “I’ve had more conversations with people who are more directly connected to the problems, and have learned that it is most important for a public servant like myself to make sure we’re looking at sensible, practical solutions.” When Favreau asked Sanders on Wednesday if he thinks that it is risky for the Democrats to put forward DSA candidates who have talked about abolishing prisons and defunding or abolishing the police, the senator replied: “What you know as well as I do is that the right wing, that’s their job, right? They will take what one person said and put, you know, $80bn of TV ads on it and make the claim every Democrat supports that.” No serious person that I know who is running for office believes in quote-unquote ‘defunding the police’,” Sanders continued. “I was a mayor for eight years, I worked very closely with cops. They have a very difficult job. Do we need police reform? Do we need to get rid of racism within police departments? Absolutely.” “But nobody I know believes in ‘defunding the police’, he added. “But a lot of this stuff, as you well know, is what the right wing plays on, and multiplies on Fox 10 times a day and through their ads,” Sanders said. “But most of the serious candidates that I know and support do not support those things.” Rumors that Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Maga congresswoman from Georgia, was about to announce the creation of a new political party with fellow exiles from the Trumpist movement, including Tucker Carlson, Thomas Massie and Joe Kent, appear to have been greatly exaggerated. However, the former congresswoman did unveil a different new venture this week: a Cameo account, where, for $150, her fans can now book Greene to deliver “unforgettable” video messages for friends or relations celebrating “a milestone birthday, an anniversary, or a long-awaited reunion”. Robert F Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services has provided a copy of Dr Anthony Fauci’s phone to a Republican-led Senate panel investigating the doctor’s role as a senior advisor on the response to the Covid-19 pandemic to presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden, the Wall Street Journal reports. Kennedy, a lawyer with no scientific training, wrote a conspiratorial, 500-page book attacking Fauci in 2021 that sold more than a million copies for a rightwing publisher – thanks in part to blurbs from fellow non-scientists Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan, Alan Dershowitz and Tony Robbins. The chair of the Senate panel, Republican Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, confirmed the report on social media. “Hopefully, this device will address many of the questions he refused to answer at last week’s hearing,” Johnson added. While delivering remarks, in English and French, about a drive to build affordable housing in Toronto on Wednesday, Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, broke off from his prepared remarks to say: “I would now like to inform you that ‌the teleprompter has ceased to function.” As the audience laughed, Carney ad-libbed a jibe about Donald Trump. “Unlike a certain world leader, I do not view this as a conspiracy,” the prime minister said, to more laughter. Last year, after his address to the United Nations general assembly was marred by technical mishaps – including a malfunctioning escalator, sound system and teleprompter – Trump suggested that he had been the victim of “triple sabotage at the UN”. Later in the event, Carney also said that Canadian trade negotiators were talking with US counterparts to find some way to avoid the implementation, in two weeks, of new tariffs imposed by Trump on a broad range of imports from Canada, on everything from alcohol and cement to hockey sticks. Carney’s mockery of Trump on Wednesday was not the first time he has made fun of the American president. Speaking in Ireland in June, Carney did a brief impression of Trump as he joked about having been presented with a ceremonial key to the White House during a visit to Washington. Moments after Nevada’s Republican governor, Joe Lombardo, stepped off stage at the midterm campaign rally hosted by Donald Trump on Wednesday, the president praised an election conspiracy theorist who is running to oversee Nevada’s elections as its secretary of state, Jim Marchant. The transition was awkward because Marchant won the Republican nomination for the office in June, narrowly defeating a candidate endorsed by Lombardo who is not an election-denier. “A very special man, I wish you’d get him in office, because he’s incredible, I’ve known him so long and he’s got to get in, he just has to,” Trump said. “He had a big victory with spending very little money because everyone respects him, Jim Marchant, he’s a candidate for secretary of state.” Marchant, who has spread baseless conspiracy theories about election fraud in Nevada for years, and previously said he would not have certified Joe Biden’s 2020 victory in the state, is attempting to unseat the Democratic incumbent, Cisco Aguilar, in a rematch of the 2022 election the Democrat won by just 23,000 votes. Jon Ralston, the chief executive of the non-profit Nevada Independent, noted with amazement Trump’s endorsement of “an unhinged conspiracy theorist who said he didn’t even trust the results of his own primary he won”. In a speech laced with anti-Muslim animus, Donald Trump just accused Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the US Senate from Michigan, who is Muslim, of being motivated by deep-seated antisemitism. El-Sayed, who narrowly won the Democratic primary in Michigan despite $30m in negative ads paid for by groups linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), has campaigned with Jewish supporters, but strongly condemned Israel’s killing and mistreatment of Palestinians. According to Trump, El-Sayed is “a hater of Jews and a hater of Israel”. “Just say this guy hates Jews. Somebody said, ‘Oh, that’s a little strong.’ No, he hates Jews and he hates Israel,” Trump said. “He’s a man of hate.” The president then mockingly pronounced El-Sayed’s name, clearly stressing its Arabic origins, eliciting boos from his supporters in Nevada, just as his earlier reference to “Barack Hussein Obama” had. At another point in the speech, Trump also made a sarcastic reference to “the lovely Islamic Republic of Iran”. Earlier on Wednesday, as other Republicans released frankly racist statements attempting to cast El-Sayed as a Muslim extremist, El-Sayed addressed Jewish Americans in comments carried live by Fox News. “To my Jewish American sisters and brothers, one of the most indelible memories of this campaign will have been the opportunity to break bread with you at seder,” El-Sayed said, “and listening to sisters and brothers who said, ‘I want to join this movement because Aipac doesn’t speak for me; because I understand that self-determination for one people does not require the quenching of self-determination for another people; that unless all of us are free, none of us are free,’ I want to tell you the great gift that you’ve given me.” “I want you to know,” he continued, “that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety, is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.” Apparently referring to these comments, which were carried live on the president’s favorite network, Trump said: “Now he’s going around saying, ‘No, I love everybody … ’ He doesn’t love everybody. Put him in office, you’re going to find out what he loves. He doesn’t love Israel. He doesn’t love Jewish people. He hates them. He hates them with a passion that burns in his heart and is not a fricking thing he can do about it. There’s not a thing he can do about it ’cause he hates them.” The idea that many non-Jews hold a deep-seated, unreasoning, anti-Jewish animus is a frequent claim made by Israeli politicians, including Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “When I watch Abdul,” Trump said later in the speech, “he’s full of shit.” Donald Trump is now speaking to supporters in Nevada, and so far he is giving a standard campaign rally speech, running through his standard boasts about how well he is doing and repeating false claims he has made again and again. The president began by claiming that he had won Nevada in the 2024 election “in a landslide”. In fact, he won the state by 46,008 votes over Kamala Harris. Four years earlier, Trump had lost the state to Joe Biden by a similar if slightly smaller margin of 33,596 votes. In a speech that was billed as a presidential address on the economy, but is in effect a midterm campaign rally for Republican candidates that support him, Trump went on to repeat a series of false claims, including: his wildly inflated estimate that $19tn has been invested by foreign businesses since he returned to office; “the economy is the greatest economy we’ve ever had by far”; the fiction that “25 million poured through our southern border” during the Biden administration. Trump also told his entirely invented tale that “the king of Saudi Arabia” told him last year: “a year ago your country was dead; it was a dead country. We never thought it was coming back. And now you have the hottest country anywhere in the world.” In fact, during his visit to Riyadh in 2025, Trump told the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, the US was “the hottest country in the world”, a claim that he previously made at least a dozen times in public comments during his first term, starting with rally speeches ahead of the 2018 midterms, and has repeated dozens of times since. Lawyers for Donald Trump asked a federal judge in Miami on Wednesday to pause an earlier order that requires financial information for 400 of his business entities to be disclosed to the BBC, as the British broadcaster works to defend itself from Trump’s $10bn defamation suit over the editing of a documentary in 2024. The earlier discovery order granted the broadcaster’s lawyers access to the financial information because, as the British legal writer David Allen Green explains, Trump had claimed that the editing of his speech to supporters on 6 January 2021, before they stormed the Capitol, had caused him massive reputational harm that cost his businesses vast sums of money. Framing the case that way let the BBC argue that it had a right to discovery on the actual state of Trump’s businesses. As Courthouse News reports, Trump’s lawyers now want to narrow the scope of his defamation claim against the broadcaster to prevent the full disclosure of his financial affairs. Life for Trump’s lawyers has not been made any easier by the fact that the president has, on at least five occasions since December, falsely claimed that the BBC did not just misleadingly edit his remarks from that day, but “used AI” to put words in his mouth that he did not say. The actual BBC edit at issue spliced together two parts of Trump’s remarks that were actually spoken 54 minutes apart, but made no use of AI and the words were spoken by him, and were not, as he has claimed again and again, “AI generated”. Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination for the US Senate seat in Michigan, beating Haley Stevens in a bitter competition that became a referendum on the changing face of the Democratic party. El-Sayed won the race by a single point, fewer than 15,000 votes, according to the Associated Press. He will now face Republican nominee Mike Rogers – who ran unopposed – for a key battleground seat that is vital for Democrats to retain in order to achieve their lofty goal of reclaiming the majority in the upper chamber of Congress. More here Democrats quickly coalesced around El-Sayed following his narrow victory, urging their fractured coalition to back him with the goal of keeping the seat blue. Stevens said she has offered her “full support” to El-Sayed, while the Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, said there is “nothing more important” than “uniting” and moving forward. More here Meanwhile, Republicans wasted no time painting El-Sayed as a vote for “complete insanity”. Rogers, the GOP nominee, said the Senate race was now about “whether Michigan has a future built on common sense – or whether we hand the keys to the most fringe extremists in the nation”. Donald Trump, for his part, said El-Sayed’s win was “great news” for Republicans, calling him a “communist loser”. Further down ballot, progressive Donavan McKinney beat incumbent Shri Thanedar in a closely watched Democratic primary for Michigan’s 13th congressional district. It was a contest that mirrored many of identity battles facing the party this midterm cycle. By a vote of 51-44, mainly along party lines, the Senate confirmed Erica Schwartz to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), after the agency has gone without a permanent director for almost a year. The previous Senate-confirmed leader – Susan Monarez – was ousted by Robert F Kennedy Jr last August, after they clashed over the health secretary’s vaccine policy. It’s worth noting that Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan was the latest win for progressives across the country, many of whom challenged establishment-backed Democrats in key races across the country. Last month, Democratic socialist Melat Kiros unseated the long-serving US representative Diana DeGette in Colorado’s primary elections. And in New York, Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, who were all backed by mayor Zohran Mamdani, also won races in the June congressional primaries. Lander won his race comfortably, defeating the two-term Democratic representative Dan Goldman. Valdez won against Antonio Reynoso – the handpicked successor of Nydia Velázquez. And Chevalier toppled Representative Adriano Espaillat, the powerful five-term incumbent who chairs the congressional Hispanic caucus. Despite progressive nominee Cori Bush’s loss in Missouri against pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell on Tuesday, Michigan insurgents in two key House races also claimed wins. A reminder that my colleagues are covering the latest developments out of the Middle East at our dedicated live blog. This includes the latest news that Iran and Oman have agreed a route for ships transiting the strait of Hormuz and are finalising the draft deal for jointly managing the vital chokepoint. However, Iran’s foreign ministry said that that any reopening of the strait would depend on the US fulfilling what Tehran sees as its commitment to end its own naval blockade of Iran’s ports. By a vote of 51-44, mainly along party lines, the Senate confirmed Erica Schwartz to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), after the agency has been without a permanent director for almost a year. Tim Kaine of Virginia was the only Democrat to join all Republicans and vote yes on Schwartz’s nomination. Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, congratulated the progressive Democrats he endorsed, who won in Michigan’s closely watched primary elections –including the Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. “Congratulations to Will Lawrence, Donavan McKinney and Dr Abdul El-Sayed on their historic victories last night,” Sanders said. The senator highlighted El-Sayed’s victory, commenting on his success despite the funding disparities between El-Sayed and his rival, Haley Stevens. “Abdul took on the entire billionaire class, faced more than $60 million in spending against him, and WON,” Sanders added in his statement on social media. During a press conference at the Department of Justice earlier today, the acting US attorney general, Todd Blanche, avoided siding with Donald Trump or the US attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, over her decision to dismiss vandalism charges at the reflecting pool against Olympic canoeist David Hearn. Blanche said that he did not want the “message” to be that “because Trump expressed appropriate frustration at the damage done to the reflecting pool” that Pirro is not “working every day to combat violent crime and to make the city safe”. These comments come as Blanche awaits the final vote in the Senate for his confirmation as attorney general. Two key Republican holdouts, senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, said they would now vote for Blanche’s nomination after he said in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Trump’s allies was dead. However, Susan Collins, a moderate Republican senator from Maine, said she would note vote to confirm Blanche – citing the creation of the so-called “anti-weaponization fund” as part of her reasoning. Blanche is hoping to gain the votes of two other GOP lawmakers in order to shore up his position – Lisa Murkowski and Bill Cassidy. Cassidy, the outgoing senator from Louisiana who lost his primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger, said in a radio interview on Wednesday that he had still not made his decision. “I’ve got to be convinced that he is an attorney general who just happens to have once been President Trump’s personal attorney, as opposed to President Trump’s personal attorney who is now the attorney general,” Cassidy said. “I think there’s a big difference between the two.” A quick note that we can expect a vote today on Erica Schwartz’s nomination to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). This would mean that the beleaguered public health agency finally has a permanent director in almost a year, since the last Senate-confirmed leader – Susan Monarez – was ousted by Robert F Kennedy Jr last August, after they clashed over the health secretary’s vaccine policy. Schwartz received a majority of the votes to advance her nomination out of the Senate health committee, and is expected to be confirmed along party lines. During her confirmation hearing Schwartz, who previously served as deputy surgeon general in Donald Trump’s first administration, was questioned about how she would handle Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism as a longstanding supporter of childhood inoculations. A former megachurch pastor who endured 15 years of conversion practices is set to become the first transgender member of Michigan’s state legislature after winning a Democratic primary election on Tuesday. Joanna Whaley comfortably defeated Frank Liberati, a former state representative, and Gary Schlack in the primary for the second district of the Michigan statehouse, a Democratic stronghold. Earlier this year Liberati sought to have Whaley disqualified from the ballot over her name change, but the Wayne county clerk’s office dismissed the challenge, finding that Whaley’s candidate affidavit was legal and proper. Whaley, 38, who grew up in a Catholic family, previously spent two decades working as a pastor at an evangelical megachurch. Sarah McBride, the first openly transgender member of the US Congress, posted on X on Wednesday: “So proud of my friend, Joanna Whaley! She faced indignities from her opponent, channeled the energy into knocking on doors, doubled down on her economic agenda, and she defeated that former Dem legislator (who took the low road against her) by 30+%! Way to go, Joanna!” Whaley, 38, who grew up in a Catholic family, previously spent two decades working as a pastor at an evangelical megachurch. Meanwhile, Democrats are reacting more positively. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, congratulated El-Sayed on his “hard-fought victory” on social media. “Trump and the GOP are trying everything to rig the rules and silence voters – but they can’t stop a Democratic Party united around working people and accountability,” the Democrat governor wrote. “On to November! Let’s take our country back.” The Republican backlash to El-Sayed’s victory continues, with the Arkansas senator Tom Cotton writing on X that “the Democratic party has lost its mind”. In a separate post, he lashed out at the Democratic senator Chris Murphy for expressing his enthusiasm for El-Sayed’s triumph, writing: “Senate Democrats are ‘excited’ for Abdul El-Sayed who proudly campaigns with extremists who say America deserved 9/11 [referring to 2019 comments from leftwing influencer Hasan Piker]. The Islamic-Marxists truly are taking over the Democratic party. We must never give them power.” The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), which spent roughly $30m in a failed effort to defeat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary, says it’s committed to opposing him in the general election, signaling plans to spend for Republican Mike Rogers. “Our members remain determined to ensure that voters reject Dr El-Sayed and his radical anti-Israel agenda in November,” the group’s statement said. “While disappointed that some of our Aipac-backed candidates did not prevail, our community is proud to support pro-Israel Democrats and Republicans who stand for our values, and we are encouraged that voters in races across this primary season continue to broadly choose leaders who support a strong US-Israel partnership,” it added. Aipac’s brand has struggled as of late to capture new voters, with El-Sayed’s victory underscoring the continued momentum of progressive candidates. But the funding power and influence of the lobbying group still remains, with some Aipac-supported candidates triumphing on Tuesday. Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers released a statement urging general election voters to make the “simple” choice between “common sense and complete insanity”, following Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow primary win for the Michigan US Senate seat. “This election isn’t just about choosing a Senator. It’s about deciding whether Michigan has a future built on common sense – or whether we hand the keys to the most fringe extremists in the nation,” said Rogers, who ran unopposed on Tuesday, and is gunning for the open seat after narrowly losing the 2024 Senate race to Elissa Slotkin. In Michigan’s 13th congressional district – which includes parts of Detroit – Donavan McKinney beat incumbent Shri Thanedar in a closely watched Democratic primary that mirrored many of identity battles facing the party this midterm cycle. McKinney, 34, a state lawmaker who received the backing of many progressives in Congress, including the Michigan representative Rashida Tlaib and the independent senator Bernie Sanders, won his race by almost four points, and successfully ousted the two-term Thanedar, 71, who was endorsed by the House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries. While some of Thanedar and McKinney’s platform policies overlap, Thanedar’s win in 2022 marked the first time the majority-Black Detroit area has not had a Black representative in Congress in years. McKinney, who was recruited by Justice Democrats – a progressive Pac – was also endorsed by some House Congressional Black caucus members, despite party leadership backing Thanedar. The new nominee was also outspoken about the war in Gaza – calling it a “genocide” while campaigning to end military aid to Israel. McKinney also campaigned alongside Abdul El-Sayed, who went on to win the Democratic nomination for Michigan’s open US Senate seat. “They spent an unprecedented amount of money to beat us” Abdul El-Sayed said, after officially winning the Michigan’s Democratic nomination for US Senate. El-Sayed remarked on the millions in outside spending while holding his first press conference in downtown Detroit as the newly minted nominee. “But it turns out the commercials are the part of the television show most people don’t want to watch,” he added. “We took on a machine. You’re not supposed to be able to beat $70m dollars of outside spending – a record amount of money spent in a campaign against a Democrat in a primary in any campaign,” he said. “You’re not supposed to be able to beat that. And what we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money.” Ahead of the Associated Press calling the Michigan Democratic primary for US Senate, various conservative groups got to work blasting Abdul El-Sayed as the likely nominee. The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) released a video on Wednesday, decidedly referring to the candidate by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and branding him as “the most radical Senate candidate in America” and “wrong for Michigan” – while highlighting comments from leftwing influencer Hasan Piker that “America deserved 9/11” during a stream in 2019. Piker has campaigned alongside El-Sayed, and routinely apologized for his past remarks. State and national Democrats have begun to coalesce around Abdul El-Sayed after he narrowly won the primary for the Michigan US Senate seat. One of Michigan’s Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin, congratulated El-Sayed and said there is “nothing more important” than “uniting, keeping this seat blue, flipping the House and Senate, and providing a real check” on Donald Trump. Others in the party have also urged the fractured coalition to work together in the short runway until November to retain a vital seat for Democrats to have any chance at reclaiming the majority in the upper chamber. “I urge folks to come together – the stakes are high, and we need Abdul in the Senate to stand up for all Michiganders and the country we love,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Marlyand. Meanwhile, Mallory McMorrow, who also ran in the Michigan Senate Democratic primary before suspending her campaign in July, said that El-Sayed has her “full endorsement and support”. McMorrow’s name still appeared on Tuesday’s ballot, and she wracked up more than 60,000 votes – all of which El-Sayed hopes to absorb in November. “This was a brutal primary,” McMorrow said. “Trump and Mike Rogers are counting on us staying divided. Let’s prove them wrong by beating Mike Rogers and taking our country back.” In Las Vegas, Donald Trump has weighed in on the results from the Democratic primary for Michigan’s US Senate seat. After Abdul El-Sayed won the party’s nomination, the president called it “great news” for Republicans in a post on Truth Social. Trump went on to call El-Sayed a “communist loser who hates Jews and Israel”, despite the Democratic nominee’s frequent denunciations of antisemitism. The president also noted that Stevens “was not expected to do nearly as well as she did”. “Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” Trump wrote. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) has said it now looks forward to working with Abdul El-Sayed in the wake of his primary victory in Michigan. The main campaign arm for Senate Democrats had backed Haley Stevens in the bitter race for the nomination, but praised El-Sayed for his “energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders across the state”. In a statement Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, and Kristen Gillibrand, chair of the DSCC, said that Democrats are united by a “common purpose” in this midterms cycle, “putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate”. They called Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee who ran unopposed in his primary, “a rubber stamp” from the president, and accused him of backing the same “reckless agenda that has driven up costs for working families”. Rogers lost his bid for Senate to Democrat Elissa Slotkin in 2024 by fewer than 20,000 votes. Haley Stevens has conceded in the hotly contested Democratic Senate primary in Michigan. The Asssociated Press called the race a short while ago. “I love Michigan and am so proud to have put up my hand to serve. I spoke with Abdul a few moments ago to offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November,” she said on social media. Stevens’ saw a deluge of outside spending to boost her campaign, including more than $30m from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby group. Abdul El-Sayed has won the Democratic nomination for the US Senate seat in Michigan, beating Haley Stevens in a bitter competition that became a referendum on the changing face of the Democratic party. El-Sayed won the race by a single point, fewer than 15,000 votes, according to the Associated Press. He will now face Republican nominee Mike Rogers – who ran unopposed – for a key battleground seat that is vital for Democrats to retain in order to achieve their lofty goal of reclaiming the majority in the upper chamber of Congress. The Democratic primary became a proxy battle between the establishment and progressive wings of the party, with El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former state public health official, receiving the backing of many leaders on the left flank. Meanwhile Stevens, a serving US congresswoman who flipped her district blue in 2018, received support from party leaders – including the Michigan governor, Gretchen Whitmer – and was supported by tens of millions of dollars in outside Pac funding from the pro-Israel lobby. The latter was a point on which El-Sayed hammered on the campaign trail in Michigan, the birthplace of the uncommitted movement – which saw a sizeable portion of Arab-American voters eschew Kamala Harris in 2024 over the Biden administration’s stance on the Israel-Gaza war. “This was always going to be the many versus the money, and tonight, we have shown that Michiganders want money out of politics, money in their pockets, and Medicare for all. We are building a coalition that is fired up and ready to go beat Mike Rogers,” said El-Sayed’s campaign manager, Alia Kapasi, in a statement. Wayne county – Michigan’s largest – is the area of the state we’re still waiting on before the Associated Press calls the race. As of now, 88% of votes in the county have been counted. A quick update on the marquee Democratic primary race for US Senate in Michigan. Haley Stevens is trailing Abdul El-Sayed by fewer than 15,000 votes, according the Associated Press, whose count the Guardian uses on election night. As of now, 96% of the votes have been counted in this extremely tight race. El-Sayed’s campaign has, nonetheless, started its victory lap and sent out emails noting that he has won. During a CNN interview on Tuesday, Miller said that the president told him Monday that “it’s going to be a tough race” but did not tell him to end his re-election campaign. Donald Trump is in Las Vegas today, where he’s set to giver a speech about the economy, and his administration’s message on affordability. In the three-month runway to the November midterms, we’ll hear a lot more from the president as he seeks to campaign on behalf of many of his preferred nominees, while defending unpopular policies that many of them have supported on the trail. All eyes may be on Michigan right now to see if progressives can win yet another race in the Democratic primary for Senate – latest numbers have Abdul El-Sayed leading at 49.43% ahead of moderate Haley Stevens with 45.85% of the vote.
